newsitem.title: GERMANY: DUISENBERG SAYS EMU STABILITY PACT VITAL TOOL - BONN.
newsitem.headline: DUISENBERG SAYS EMU STABILITY PACT VITAL TOOL - BONN.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg said on Wednesday he supported a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty to govern which countries join Europe's single currency project in 1999.

Duisenberg, who takes over this summer as chief of the European Monetary Institute (EMI) -- forerunner to a European central bank -- also said lasting fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria was vital to ensure the euro currency will be stable.

"Considering the need to create a stable monetary union I would, as president of the Dutch central bank and of the future EMI, draw your attention to the significance of a strict interpretation of the convergence criteria," he said.
"We would only be able to create a stable currency union if we manage to fulfil the convergence criteria not for just one year, but permanently."
Duisenberg's comments were taken from a speech he was due to give to a Friedrich Ebert foundation forum on European monetary union (EMU).

Duisenberg is a leading candidate to take over at the planned supra-national central bank. He said its independence from political interference must be assured to ensure that the euro is a strong and stable currency.

In the Maastricht treaty, he noted, "it is forbidden to give orders to the ECB or to try to influence its directors. That does not, by the way, prevent central bank directors from exchanging views with their finance ministers."
Duisenberg also said the so-called stability pact, a mechanism to enforce budgetary discipline, offered important guarantees for sound state finances within EMU.
"A key element of this pact is that countries both within and outside EMU must commit to achieving a budget position which is almost in balance or even in surplus," he said.

"A budget which on average is close to balance creates room to cope with cyclical and non-cyclical shocks, without the deficit overstepping the limit of three percent of GDP defined in the the treaty."
"The pact is thus not rigid, but creates room for manoeuvre within the limits defined by the Maastricht treaty," he said.

Duisenberg urged other European countries to copy the policies adopted by the Netherlands in the early 1980s which he said had made it possible to tie the guilder to the mark, cut the budget deficit, reduce national debt and still create jobs.
"This policy has not achieved its final goal, because there are still too many people without work and public debt is still too high. But we are going in the right direction," he said.
Referring to Germany, he said that Bonn's efforts to meet the Maastricht fiscal criteria illustrated that European states above all are having problems meeting the budget criteria.
But, if countries manage to control borrowing, they can create a virtuous cycle which reduces interests, cuts debt costs, boosts investor confidence and leads to lower inflation.
"As I said, countries can only join the third stage who fit into a stable monetary union. Countries prove that with achievements which demonstrate lasting convergence," he said.

In remarks apparently directed at countries like Italy or Spain, he said: "Countries should not treat qualification as a sprint race...Rather, they should kick bad habits like big budget deficits, which are like too much smoking and drinking."

And, Duisenberg added, countries who do not make it into the first round of EMU still have time to meet the convergence criteria in order to be in in the currency club in time for the planned launch of cash euros in 2002.
"The euro is a common European adventure, which will only be over when all, or nearly all, (European Union) member states take part," he said.
-- Douglas Busvine, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150
